title: OilRig
summary: OilRig, tracked by vendors as APT34, Helix Kitten, COBALT GYPSY and Hazel Sandstorm, is an espionage group whose activity public reporting associates with Iranian state interests. Targets concentrate in the Middle East, particularly government, energy, telecommunications and financial organisations, and the group has also used third parties as stepping stones into their clients. Reported tradecraft includes custom backdoors, heavy use of built-in scripting such as PowerShell, credential harvesting, and command and control carried over domain name system queries so that the traffic resembles ordinary name resolution. Operators are reported to approach employees directly through social media and messaging platforms. Detection depends on unusual name resolution patterns, script execution logs, and mailbox rules created without the user's knowledge. Attribution rests on targeting, tooling and infrastructure, and should be presented with the confidence its source states.

beginner.definition: OilRig is a name for a spying group that public reports link to Iranian state interests. It mainly targets government and energy organisations in the Middle East. The group writes its own tools and also uses features that already exist in the operating system, so it leaves fewer obvious files behind. Other security companies call the same activity APT34 or Helix Kitten.
beginner.whyItMatters: Built-in tools are already on your computers, so you cannot simply block them. The group also works through trusted suppliers to reach their clients, which spreads the damage further than expected. If your staff discuss work with strangers on social media, that conversation can become the entry point. Watching how internal tools are used is far more useful than watching only for known malware files.
howItWorks: Operators find employees through public profiles and start a work-related conversation online.
They send a file or link that appears to be a document, a tool or a job offer.
Once opened, a small script runs and connects back through ordinary network services.
In some cases the connection hides inside name lookups, which almost every network allows.
The group collects passwords and mailbox rules, then uses them to reach other systems.
They may use a partner company as a bridge into the real target's network.
beginner.example: Picture a large office where every visitor signs in at the front desk. Now imagine someone who never enters the building at all. They telephone the front desk and ask for a package to be passed upstairs. The desk follows normal procedure, and the package reaches the right floor. OilRig often works through a trusted partner in the same way, letting someone else carry the package inside.
takeaways: Built-in administration tools can be abused, so monitor how they are used.
Name resolution traffic deserves attention in network monitoring.
A supplier can carry an intrusion into your network without knowing it.

objectives: Describe the regional focus and reported state nexus of OilRig.
Explain how command and control can hide inside name resolution traffic.
Describe the role of social engineering aimed at employees online.
Identify mailbox and script execution evidence that points to this activity.
Explain the risk of a third party being used as an access path.
